content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"The lost sheep primarily symbolizes the individual sinner (and straying humanity generally) who has wandered from God and is sought, found, and joyfully restored by God/Christ the Good Shepherd (Luke 15:3-7; Matt 18:12-14; Isa 53:6). All responses list, as a common secondary reading, the 'lost sheep of the house of Israel' — covenant Israel strayed and lacking faithful shepherds (Matt 10:6; 15:24; Jer 50:6; Ezek 34).","book_summary":"The lost sheep are the scattered house of Israel, whom God seeks and regathers — a collective national identification, keyed to Matthew 15:24 and cross-referenced to a chapter on Jacob, Israel & Ephraim (suggesting a scattered-tribes/regathering framework).","consensus_core_identification":"Any spiritually straying person/sinner sought and restored by the divine Shepherd, with Israel as a common contextual sub-reading.","book_core_identification":"The scattered house of Israel specifically, sought and regathered by God.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"BOOK_SUBSET","boundary_disagreement":"The book restricts the referent to national/corporate Israel (scattered and to be regathered), excluding the consensus's dominant cases: the generic individual sinner, straying humanity, and the backslidden church member. It elevates what consensus treats as a common secondary, context-specific reading (Matt 10:6; 15:24) to the sole identification, and the 'regathered' language plus the Ephraim chapter cross-reference hints at a scattered-tribes emphasis that Response A flags as a rare/fringe extension.","material_contradiction":"None at the core: 'strayed ones whom God seeks' remains intact; the dispute is over whose straying the symbol denotes, not whether the symbol means straying-and-divine-seeking.","rationale":"The book's identification is a recognized consensus alternative (labeled 'common' in all four responses), so it does not replace the consensus category of strayed sheep sought by God; it narrows the extension from any sinner to corporate Israel. This is a real boundary disagreement — the book implicitly rejects the universal-sinner reading of Luke 15/Matthew 18 as the primary sense — but not a contradiction of the central image. Hence REFINED with BOOK_NARROWS and BOOK_SUBSET. If the full chapter identifies the lost sheep with the literal lost ten tribes or modern peoples, that would push toward the rare reading noted in Response A, but the glossary entry alone stays within the mainstream Israel alternative.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"Matthew 15:24 explicitly says Jesus was sent 'unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel,' so one could argue the book's identification is not a narrowing but the plain textual meaning of that verse, making it EQUIVALENT for the Matthean usage; however, the consensus term covers the broader biblical image (Luke 15, Isa 53:6, Ps 119:176), and the book's single-verse basis does not establish the 'regathered' scattered-Israel emphasis, nor does it address the dominant sinner/repentance usage.","confidence":"high"}
